beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Too Convinced to Stop asks how ambitious beliefs can remain answerable to evidence.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book judges the process before success or failure rewrites the story.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It follows founders and institutions through confidence, authority, dissent, and the distribution of costs.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its category of impossible certainty is explicitly nonclinical.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers gain questions for distinguishing bold experimentation from organizational protection against correction.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: An ambitious claim may need time before a decisive test becomes possible.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book asks whether that interval buys learning or merely extends the protective story.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Evidence debt grows when confidence outruns what a project can presently substantiate.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A corrigible founder preserves channels through which unwelcome findings can change the plan.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The distinction concerns how belief behaves under pressure, not whether ambition looks unusual.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Success can make earlier recklessness look wise, while failure can erase a responsible experiment.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book therefore separates outcomes from the quality of decisions available beforehand.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It asks who could challenge the claim and who would bear the losses.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A failed venture is not automatically fraud or evidence of psychological pathology.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: These distinctions make its organizational cases useful without reducing them to stories about exceptional personalities.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Begin with the nonclinical definition and the distinction between confidence and resistance to correction.
